Title: Got Lactose?
Content: As baby mammals grow up, they stop drinking their mothers’ milk and their bodies stop producing lactase, the enzyme needed to break down lactose, a carbohydrate in milk. Most mammals do not continue to produce lactase as adults and do not drink milk.

Humans are unique in that, as adults, some of them continue to drink the milk from cows or other mammals. This is possible because they continue to produce lactase. However, approximately `65%` of the adult human population cannot digest it.
The map below shows how the ability to digest lactose varies in different parts of the world.

The enzyme lactase breaks down lactose into `text(two)` simple sugars: glucose and galactose. These simple sugars then diffuse into the blood and can be used by the body. When a person who cannot digest lactose drinks milk, the undigested lactose passes from the small intestine into the large intestine. Bacteria break the lactose down, releasing several gases and other products, which may cause bloating, flatulence, and diarrhea.

`text(Two)` students, `text(A)` and `text(B)`, wanted to know if they were able to digest lactose. `text(One)` test to determine this is to monitor blood glucose levels for an `text(hour)` after drinking milk. The blood glucose test results for the students are shown in Chart `text(One)` below.

The students learned that another way to test for the ability to digest lactose is the hydrogen breath test. `text(One)` of the gases the bacteria in the large intestine produce as they break down undigested lactose is hydrogen. Hydrogen and other gases can leave the body as flatulence.

These gases can also leave the body by diffusing into the blood and be eliminated by way of the lungs. Chart `text(Two)` shows the results of the hydrogen test for the same `text(two)` students, `text(A)` and `text(B)`, after drinking milk.
